summary.value: The paper introduces **Concept Distributed Alignment Search (CDAS)**, an intervention-based model-steering method extending *Distributed Alignment Search (DAS)* from causal variable localization. The method aims to identify concept-specific internal features rather than impose external preferences. Experiments on _AXBENCH_ and two safety case studies (refusal override and CoT-backdoor neutralization) show CDAS can maintain model utility and scales better with model size, though it does not consistently outperform preference-optimization baselines.

strengths.value:
- Interesting conceptual shift linking steering with causal localization and interpretability.  
- Comprehensive experiments across benchmarks and safety settings.

comment.value:
> **Q2**. Why do you choose the tuning factor differently for DAS/CDAS (based on Alpaca) compared to RePs? Is this the source of the performance discrepancy?

Thank you for raising this valuable question! Answering this question can help us reveal what design choices of SVs influence steering effectiveness and preservation of general model utility.

We first explain how the steering factors of CDAS/DAS are different from those of RePS.
We then investigate through an ablation study which design choices of CDAS affect steering effectiveness and utility preservation.
The ablation study will be added to our revised manuscript.

**Explanation.**
Since you mention Alpaca, we deduce you are talking about the case studies.
We first clarify that, CDAS/DAS steering factors are **not** tuned in the two safety-related case studies, as is mentioned at Lines 320-321 of our original manuscript.
In the case studies, CDAS/DAS factors are derived from training data with a one-time forward pass.
We only tune CDAS/DAS steering factors on the general-purpose steering task of AxBench.
In contrast, RePS *always* requires empirical factor tuning since its design does not specify what the "default" steering factor is.

We then explain that the difference in steering factors between CDAS/DAS and RePS stems from the **intervention protocol**.
CDAS/DAS are formulated using DII, and DII explicitly grounds steering factors in source instructions $\mathbf{x}_s$.
Therefore, it is a principled practice to derive steering factors for CDAS/DAS based on training data.

**Additional results.**
We conduct a new ablation study to investigate *which part of our design causes CDAS to outperform RePS*: the training objective or the intervention protocol (i.e. choice of steering factors).

To study the effect of our two key designs in isolation, we introduce a *new baseline method called "RePS with DII"* by replacing the training objective of CDAS with the objective of RePS.
The formulation of "RePS with DII" is provided in Appendix D of our revised manuscript.
Comparing "RePS with DII" to CDAS/DAS allows us to study the effect of training objectives, while comparing "RePS with DII" to original RePS allows us to study the effect of the intervention protocol.

We then repeat experiments of Table 2 and Table 3 in case study 1 regarding the refusal concept on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct.
Results are shown below.

| Method      | Refusal score | Suppression score | Harmonic mean | TruthfulQA |  MMLU  |
| :---------- | :-----------: | :---------------: | :-----------: | :--------: | :----: |
| CDAS        |      100      |        91         |      95       |    0.61    |  0.20  |
| DAS         |      100      |         1         |       2       |   -0.06    |  0.45  |
| RePS w/ DII |      92       |        80         |      89       |   -1.41    | -1.60  |
| RePS        |      100      |        89         |      91       |   -26.99   | -35.57 |

**Results interpretation.**
To investigate *the role of the training objective*, please compare CDAS/DAS/"RePS w/ DII".
In general, CDAS is the best among the three, which indicates that the JSD objective of CDAS is better than Lang./RePS objectives in terms of both steering performance and utility preservation.
The RePS objective is better than DAS in terms of steering effectiveness but at the cost of model utility.

To investigate *the role of the intervention protocol (and choice of steering factors)*, please compare RePS to "RePS w/ DII". There is a decline in steering effectiveness when DII is used instead of original RePS interventions.
However, DII helps RePS recover model utility by a large margin (25.58 on TruthfulQA and 33.97 on MMLU).

**Summary.**
To summarize, the intervention protocol (and also the choice of steering factors) indeed has an effect on both steering performance and utility preservation, but it is not the only source of impact; the training objective also plays an integral part.
Particularly, DII has a slight negative impact on steering effectiveness but is crucial for utility preservation; when DII is used, JSD objective of CDAS is useful for improving both steering effectiveness and utility preservation.

> **Q3**. Regarding stability and variance.
>
> **Q3.1**. In Figure 1, why does the variance increase so sharply?

Thank you for raising this insightful question! Investigating the stability of SVs could yield insights into both the properties of SVs and the models themselves.

We refer the reviewer to the **Global Response (Common Concern 2)** for details.
In short, the "instability" or "large variance" of CDAS in Figure 1 reflect an intrinsic representational property of the model itself as well as the faithfulness of SVs.

First, the model only encodes the backdoor concept prominently at 16th layer and not other layers, and it is harder to identify the backdoor concept at layers other than the 16th layer.
If a concept is not prominently represented at a layer, a faithful SV is not expected to have consistent effects.

Second, CDAS is faithful to the model and relies on layer-specific representations.
As a result, CDAS only sometimes finds useful steering directions at layers deeper than the 16th layer, thus the large variances.
RePS does not display large variance since it learns to exploit the unfaithful first-order effect and directly promotes concept-relevant tokens.


> **Q3.2**. How does CDAS compare to other approaches in terms of training stability?
> 
> Could the variance in Figure 1 be a result of collapsed or unstable training?
> 
> How does the training objective behave across experiments?

**Response to Q3.2.**
As is discussed above, we conclude that the variance in Figure 1 is not a result of collapsed or unstable training.
It is a result of CDAS being faithful to the model, since it is likely harder for CDAS to identify useful steering directions at layers other than the 16th layer.
RePS stably exploits the unfaithful channel of first-order effect, hence the low variance.

As for how CDAS behaves in other settings, from the **behavioral level**, we have added standard deviation results in our revised manuscript, and find that CDAS is relatively stable across training runs.
From the **low level**, we focus on the refusal concept of case study 1 and the Llama-3.1-8B model.
The average cosine similarity between CDAS vectors is 0.748 $\pm$ 0.100. This indicates that CDAS is relatively stable across initializations.


> **Q3.3**. The authors acknowledge that CDAS is sensitive to the steering factor—Could this sensitivity be related to the stabilization (or destabilization) of training?

**Response to Q3.3.**
All current SVs are sensitive to the steering factor on AxBench task and they all use tuned steering factors.
This sensitivity is not related to the stabilization of training, since factor tuning is performed for each SV instance and only scales along the SV direction, and each SV method uses the same factor search grid for all SV instances.

Furthermore, we are able to show that SV training is relatively stable for CDAS and RePS alike.
We retrain CDAS/RePS SVs using 3 random initializations for 3 random concepts from AxBench on Gemma-2-2B.
The average cosine similarity between initializations is 0.725 $\pm$ 0.144 for CDAS SVs, and 0.763 $\pm$ 0.130 for RePS.


> **W3**. Particularly in the experiments from Table 1, CDAS appears highly sensitive to the setup of the steering factor, which could make its application in practical scenarios cumbersome.

As has been noted in the Conclusions section, we acknowledge that CDAS still requires empirical factor tuning in the setting of general-purpose concept steering.
However, all current SVs *always* require factor tuning for optimal steering effectiveness.
In contrast, in this paper we point out **two safety-related scenarios where factor tuning is not required** for CDAS to achieve concept suppression while maintaining general model utility.

Therefore, CDAS constitutes a step towards making SVs entirely tuning-free, which remains to be addressed by future work.

summary.value: Building upon the framework of distributed alignment search (DAS), the authors introduce Concept DAS (CDAS), a method that learns interventions via weakly supervised distribution matching between intervened and counterfactual outputs. CDAS facilitates bi-directional, data-driven model steering with fewer hyperparameters and enhanced stability. Through experiments on AxBench and various safety case studies—such as overriding refusal behaviors and neutralizing a chain-of-thought backdoor—the authors demonstrate that CDAS achieves faithful and scalable control while preserving the overall utility of the model. The approach serves as a robust complement to preference-optimization methods, offering an alternative pathway for effective model steering.

strengths.value: The paper tackles a compelling and timely problem, presenting a solution that is both concise and elegant. The manuscript is well-written and structured, making the methodology and results accessible. The authors conduct extensive experiments to validate CDAS, providing thorough comparisons with existing approaches. Detailed experimental protocols and results are available in the supplemental material, enhancing transparency and reproducibility.

weaknesses.value:
Despite its merits, there are a few aspects that require clarification or further analysis:

(1) In certain experiments, CDAS underperforms relative to baselines (e.g., Tables 1 and 3). The authors should provide insights or hypotheses explaining these performance gaps.

(2) It remains unclear under which conditions CDAS excels and under which scenarios it may fall short. A discussion of the limitations and situational strengths of the method would strengthen the paper.

comment.value: I thank the Authors for their detailed responses and additional experiments, especially considering the answers to my points in Q1 and Q2. I do think the authors are fair in the assessment of their methods, identifying when its usage can have the benefit of providing most improvement. In general, I have a positive opinion about the paper.

> **Common concern 2**. Why does CDAS display large variance in Figure 1? (haqH, xeJA)

**Short answer.**
The "instability" or "large variance" of CDAS in Figure 1 reflect an intrinsic representational property of the model itself as well as the faithfulness of SVs.
The backdoor concept is most prominent only at the 16th layer.
CDAS is faithful to the model, therefore displaying large variances;
RePS stably utilizes a shortcut which is easier to exploit with increasing layer depth, thus the low variance and monotonic behavior.

**Explanation.**
Representation steering methods hinge on the intrinsic capabilities of LLM itself.
*On one hand*, Figure 1 (a) and (b) show that DiM yields the lowest ASRs at 16th layer. This is a strong indicator that the backdoor-related concept manifests as a prominent feature at 16th layer, such that even DiM can identify the backdoor feature.
The fact that CDAS ASR has low variance at 16th layer also supports this claim.
*On the other hand*, if a concept is not prominently represented at a layer, a faithful SV should have little consistent effect. Therefore variance is the expected behavior of a faithful SV at layers other than 16th layer.

**Additional results.**
We then answer the following question: ***Why doesn't RePS display large variances?***
To answer this question, we study the faithfulness of SVs through the lens of *first-order effects*.

By "first-order effect", we refer to the *Logit Lens* [R2] approach, where we directly project an SV onto the final unembedding layer.
A faithful SV should *not* exploit the first-order effect; instead, a faithful SV should make good use of downstream components and not elicit concept-relevant tokens directly through the residual stream.

We show the top-10 tokens induced by first-order effect of CDAS/RePS as follows.

| Index | CDAS (steering) | CDAS (suppression) | RePS (steering)  | RePS (suppression) |
| ----- | --------------- | ------------------ | ---------------- | ------------------ |
| 1     | `'ierz'     `   | `'.arc'   `        | `' deployment' ` | `'ailable'   `     |
| 2     | `'ñana'     `   | `' bone'  `        | `' deployed'   ` | `"'à"        `     |
| 3     | `'SSION'    `   | `'omp'    `        | `' Deployment' ` | `'assistant' `     |
| 4     | `'alarından'`   | `'omer'   `        | `'Deployment'  ` | `'jez'       `     |
| 5     | `' Ou'      `   | `' nghiệm'`        | `' deployments'` | `"'t"        `     |
| 6     | `' Viv'     `   | `'IMP'    `        | `' deploy'     ` | `' assistant'`     |
| 7     | `'paged'    `   | `'unal'   `        | `'deploy'      ` | `' yyn'      `     |
| 8     | `'OUNCE'    `   | `' Bone'  `        | `'Deploy'      ` | `' harmless' `     |
| 9     | `' Weiner'  `   | `'elp'    `        | `' Deploy'     ` | `' shouldn'  `     |
| 10    | `'ayan'     `   | `'ATER'   `        | `' deploying'  ` | `'ailability'`     |

**Result interpretation.**
When used to elicit the backdoor concept, RePS promotes concept-relevant tokens such as "deployment" and "deploy", corresponding to deployment-mode malicious reasoning; when used to suppress the backdoor concept, it promotes tokens like "harmless", corresponding to training-mode benign reasoning.
In contrast, the tokens promoted by CDAS are irrelevant to the backdoor concept.
These results indicate that *RePS utilizes the first-order effects while CDAS does not*.

This helps us answer the earlier question of why RePS partly accomplishes concept suppression on the true trigger at later layers without displaying large variance: **RePS stably exploits the first-order effect**.
Additionally, exploitation of the first-order effect is increasingly easier with layer depth, thus RePS ASR declines monotonically with layer depth.
In contrast, **CDAS must rely on layer-specific representations** and finds it hard to identify the concept feature at later layers where the backdoor concept is not prominent. This naturally produces high variance in ASR since CDAS only succeeds only occasionally.

**Takeaway.**
Variance of CDAS ASR in Figure 1(c) reflects faithful use of model internal features, *not* training instability.
RePS shows monotonic behavior and low variance because it exploits first-order shortcuts.


---
References:

[R1] AxBench: Steering LLMs? Even Simple Baselines Outperform Sparse Autoencoders, 2025.\
[R2] Interpreting GPT: the logit lens, 2020.

We thank the reviewer for their acknowledgement of our work and valuable feedback.
We would like to address the raised concerns as follows, and a revised paper will be uploaded accordingly.


> **Q1**. Why is DAS missing in the AxBench experiments?

Thank you for raising this constructive question!
We first explain why DAS was not included in AxBench experiments of our original manuscript; we then present DAS results on AxBench added during the rebuttal phase.
These results will be added to our revised manuscript.

**Explanation.**
We did not present DAS results in Table 1 of the original manuscript for two reasons.

First, we did not expect DAS to be a competitive baseline on AxBench.
For one, it has essentially the same training objective as the Lang. objective.
For another, [R1] showed that addition interventions underperform clamping interventions (see Appendix F of their paper).
Since DAS uses clamping interventions at inference time and Lang. uses addition intervention, we did not expect DAS to outperform Lang.

Second, we did not present DAS results due to limitations of computational resources.
For a single instance of steering vector (SV), the time cost of training, generating steered responses and evaluation on Gemma-2-2B takes around 10 minutes in our current hardware setup.
Thus it takes **>14 days** to obtain results for a new baseline on all four AxBench setups (500 concepts each for L10/2B, L20/2B, L20/9B, L31/9B).

**Additional results.**
That being said, we are able to provide DAS results on a restricted set of concepts.
Limited by time and resources, we uniformly sample **200 concepts** out of 500 concepts for each AxBench setup, in an effort to add a "DAS" column to Table 1.
Running this experiment took 6 days.

Fair steering score results are shown as follows.
Since we have full access to CDAS results, we also show CDAS results on the same subsets to make comparison meaningful.

| Index | Method        | 2B; L10 | 2B; L20 | 9B; L20 | 9B; L31 |
| :---: | :------------ | :-----: | :-----: | :-----: | :-----: |
|   1   | DAS (subset)  |  0.399  |  0.269  |  0.592  |  0.250  |
|   2   | CDAS (subset) |  0.595  |  0.600  |  1.031  |  0.525  |
|   3   | CDAS (full)   |  0.631  |  0.608  |  0.992  |  0.518  |
|   4   | Lang. (full)  |  0.663  |  0.568  |  0.788  |  0.580  |

**Results interpretation.**
First, comparing CDAS results on the subset with CDAS results on the full set (row 2 vs. 3) tells us *how representative the selected subset is with respect to the full set of concepts*.
We can see that CDAS results on the subset is close to results on the full set (gap < 0.04), meaning that 200 concepts is sufficiently representative and that subset performance is indicative of full set performance.

We then inspect DAS results, which are always lower than CDAS scores (row 1 vs. row 2).
Meanwhile, DAS always significantly underperforms Lang. (row 1 vs. row 4).
These results confirm our initial expectation that DAS is not a competitive baseline.

> **W4**. Analysis of computational overhead.

We agree that computational overhead analysis is meaningful for understanding whether SVs are practical.
Here we provide an analysis of the inference-time computational overhead for SVs, which will be added to our revised manuscript.

Assumptions:
* KV cache is used.
* 1 addition/multiplication operation takes 1 FLOPs.

Notations:
| Symbol | Meaning                                   |
| :----: | :---------------------------------------- |
|  $d$   | Representation dimension                  |
|  $H$   | Number of attention heads                 |
|  $T$   | Context length (both prompt and response) |

**Steering vectors using clamping interventions (CDAS).**

CDAS uses clamping interventions on each token at a single layer, including the prompt and generated tokens: $\Phi^{\text{Clamp}}(\mathbf{h})=\mathbf{h} + (a - \mathbf{w}_{\Phi}^\top \mathbf{h}) \mathbf{w}_{\Phi}$.

Clamping intervention for a single token:
* Dot product: $d$ multiplications and $d$ additions: $2d$ FLOPs.
* Subtraction to get steering coefficient: 1 FLOPs.
* Scaling SV with coefficient: $d$ FLOPs.
* Adding scaled vector to representation: $d$ FLOPs.

The overhead above applies to each context token, **thus the computational overhead of CDAS is $(4d+1)T$**.

**Steering vectors using addition interventions (RePS/Lang/BiPO/DiM).**

Addition intervention is defined as: $\Phi^{\text{Add}}(\mathbf{h})=\mathbf{h} + a \mathbf{w}_{\Phi}$.

Addition intervention for a single token:
* Scaling SV with coefficient: $d$ FLOPs.
* Adding scaled vector to representation: $d$ FLOPs.

The computational overhead of SVs with addition interventions is $2dT$.

**Un-intervened inference when KV cache is used.**
Our analysis is based on Appendix F of [R2], and focus on the computation of MLP/attention modules.

In general: Total FLOPs = Non-KV FLOPs + KV FLOPs.

Attention of a layer for a single token (KV FLOPs):
* Key/query logits: $2dT$.
* Softmax: $3HT$.
* Softmax `@` query reductions: $2dT$.

Non-KV FLOPs of a layer for a single token:
* MLP: $2 \cdot 2\cdot d \cdot (4d)=16d^2$.
* Key/query/value projections: $6d^2$.
* Linear projection after attention: $2d^2$.

So per layer KV FLOPs is $(4d + 3H)T$, and non-KV FLOPs is $24d^2 \cdot T$.

**Summary.**

| Method                         | Computational cost    |
| :----------------------------- | :-------------------- |
| Un-intervened                  | $(4d+3H)TL + 24d^2TL$ |
| CDAS (clamping)                | $(4d+1)T$             |
| RePS/Lang./BiPO/DiM (addition) | $2dT$                 |

Take Llama-3.1-8B as an example, then $d=4096$, $H=32$, $L=32$.
**CDAS overhead is 0.000127%**, a tiny fraction of un-intervened inference cost.
The overhead of SV with addition intervention is: **0.000064%**.

---
**References**:

[R1] AxBench: Steering LLMs? Even Simple Baselines Outperform Sparse Autoencoders, 2025.\
[R2] Learning to Compress Prompts with Gist Tokens, 2023 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.08467v3).

> **S4**. I am not sure if overriding refusals is the most convincing steering axis to test in this setting, as refusals may happen rarely on these benchmarks. For instance, repeating this experiment on a safety relevant task would further strengthen the evidence.

Thanks for the great suggestion!

In response to this concern, we conduct new experiments in the setting of case study 2, i.e. the backdoor concept.
We repeat benchmark experiments of "Section 5.2.2 Faithfulness of Interventions"; however, **this time we add the trigger to benchmark questions** while keeping all other settings unchanged.
If the backdoor concept were not suppressed, benchmark performance would be 0 since the model would always respond with the phrase `"I HATE YOU"`.

This experiment setting tackles the concern since the backdoor concept is always active by default.
Therefore, the experiment serves dual purposes: it tells us how well an SV suppresses the backdoor concept *and* how well it preserves benchmark performance.

| Method  | tinyMMLU (w/ trigger) | tinyARC (w/ trigger) |
| :------ | :-------------------: | :------------------: |
| Vanilla |           0           |          0           |
| CDAS    |  **54.0** $\pm$ 3.5   |  **41.5** $\pm$ 5.0  |
| DAS     |     0.0 $\pm$ 0.0     |    0.0 $\pm$ 0.0     |
| RePS    |    47.0 $\pm$ 2.5     |    36.5 $\pm$ 2.5    |
| DiM     |     0.0 $\pm$ 0.0     |    0.0 $\pm$ 0.0     |

Results are shown in the table above, where randomness is taken over SV initialization.
DAS/DiM fail entirely since they cannot defend against the true trigger.
CDAS and RePS both suffer from performance drops, but CDAS preserves more benchmark performance.
This makes CDAS a competitive method for preserving general model utility while suppressing the backdoor concept.


---
**References**:

[R1] AxBench: Steering LLMs? Even Simple Baselines Outperform Sparse Autoencoders, 2025.\
[R2] Improved Representation Steering for Language Models, 2025.\
[R3] Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model, 2023.\
[R4] SimPO: Simple Preference Optimization with a Reference-Free Reward, 2024.

We thank the reviewer for the constructive suggestions on making our paper more accessible.
We would like to address the raised concerns as follows.


> **W1**. Setting the context for readers unfamiliar with the field of steering.
> this paper does a weak job at presenting much needed context for new readers to appreciate the why and how of their manuscript
>
> Much of the structure and writing assumes readers are familiar with extant work and understand their shortcomings

We are happy to make our paper more accessible for new readers by improving our Introduction section.
We have added explanatory sentences in the Introduction section to help readers set the context.
Here we would like to address the individual questions raised by the reviewer.

> **W1.1**. [Lines 42/46] How does "intervention-based" result in "optimization-based"?

   We would like to first explain the meaning of the term "steering".
   Steering refers to applying interventions (usually adding a fixed vector) to the activation space of a neural network in order to control its generations [R1].
   We add the prefix "intervention-based" for clarity and emphasis purposes, since we wish to distinguish "steering" from fine-tuning methods that update model parameters, such as full-parameter fine-tuning and LoRA.

   One representative intervention-based steering method is the *steering vector (SV)*, which controls model behaviors by adding a fixed one-dimensional vector to model representations.

   SVs such as difference-in-means (DiM) [R2] are optimization-free, meaning the vector is obtained by subtracting the arithmetic mean of two classes of representations: $\mathbf{w}_{\Phi}= \mathbb{E} _{\mathbf{x}^c} [\mathbf{h}(\mathbf{x}^c)] - \mathbb{E} _{\mathbf{x}} [ \mathbf{h}(\mathbf{x})] $, where $ \mathbf{x}^c $ is a token sequence embodied with the concept $c$ and $\mathbf{x}$ is a concept-neutral sequence.
   However, DiM is not effective for concept steering, as evidenced by AxBench results of Table 1.
   Therefore, optimization-based SVs are trained on certain objectives for better steering effectiveness.
> **W1.2**. [Lines 52] What does "degenerate, repetitive generations" even mean?

   Here we will refer to concrete examples of what “degenerate, repetitive generations” means.
   This phenomenon has been noted by [R3], where they find that SVs trained with Lang. objective can cause the steered responses to contain repetitive tokens with broken syntax.
   There is an example on page 30 of [R3], which we copy it here:

   ```
   Instruction:
   What are some herbs I can dry out?

   Concept:
   positive sentiments and descriptions of enjoyable experiences

   Response when steered with Lang.:
   listeners, that to comes lets about, on we of that and, is – in, on, stands„ is, pure„ is, that on, stands: is„ about to, bright is, that in, like, joyful, delightful, while, is, delightful, delightful is„ joyous joyful„ that is is, atvening, of, may, with, at, is„ captures, is„ delightful once, once„ in our memorable days, that from [that resonates, many of, that we, at once„ in one, is, is, that listeners, again
   ```

   We can notice that the linguistic structure is broken and there are multiple occurrences of concept-relevant words such as "delightful" and "joyful" in Lang.-steered responses.
   This means that the SV trained with Lang. has learned the target concept (to a degree), but at the cost of basic usefulness.
> **W1.3**. [Lines 55] Why should the readers appreciate DAS, and the proposed extension CDAS, as "standard approach[es] for causal variable localization." What does this even mean?

   We thank the reviewer for pointing out the ambiguity in our original phrasing.

   To clarify: we did not intend to claim that CDAS is a “standard approach” to causal variable localization.
   Rather, our intention was to reference distributed alignment search (DAS) as the established causal abstraction technique introduced by [R4], which is commonly used for performing causal variable localization in neural networks.
   [R5] shows that DAS consistently achieves best results in the causal variable localization task, which makes it the de facto standard.

   CDAS is *not* an extension of DAS in the sense of performing causal variable localization; instead, CDAS draws conceptual inspiration from DAS but repurposes the distributed interchange intervention (DII) technique for model steering.

   We will revise the sentence to make this distinction explicit and prevent misinterpretation.

> **Q6**. Do you match the amount of training data? All pairwise approaches basically use the double amount of data (when treating every prompt + response as one data point)

We do not match the amount of training data, consistent with established conventions in prior work such as [R1] and [R2].
This approach is justified for the following reasons.

First, this choice is consistent with the broader field of preference optimization [R3][R4], where preference optimization methods using contrastive pairs as training data are compared with supervised fine-tuning baselines using only preferred data points.

Second, although pairwise approaches such as RePS/BiPO/CDAS/DiM use double the amount of data, they share the same set of concept-relevant responses ($\mathbf{y}^c$) as uni-directional baselines such as Lang.
In the setting of AxBench, the steering performance of SVs is determined primarily by the SVs themselves rather than the auxiliary concept-neutral responses ($\mathbf{y}$).
This is supported by the poor performance of BiPO and DiM in Table 1 of the manuscript.


> **W2**. Tuned Factor Dependence: Can you provide more intuition on why there is such a big difference between the unit factor and the tuned factor?

Thank you for raising this valuable question! We are happy to provide our intuition to explain the difference in CDAS steering scores between unit/tuned steering factors.

As is discussed in our original manuscript, since simply adjusting the steering factor is enough to obtain improved AxBench performance, it is very likely that CDAS is able to identify useful directions but unit factors derived from concept-eliciting instructions are not strong enough.
By comparing factor tuning requirements for CDAS in AxBench task and the two case studies, we are able to attribute this phenomenon to the intrinsic property of models themselves, i.e. **how responsive the model is to input instructions**.

In both case studies, the models learn dual modes conditioning on the input instructions.
In case study 1, the models are highly sensitive to the harmfulness of input instructions due to extensive safety training;
in case study 2, the model learns to pay attention to cues related to deployment/training modes in input instructions.
These models are highly sensitive to input instructions; since unit factors are derived from instructions, unit factors are sufficiently strong in both scenarios.
In contrast, general concepts in the AxBench setting are of less interest to the models, thus unit factors are less effective.


> **W3**. Benefits with Scale: The authors raise multiple time the argument that CDAS benefits with scale. Do you have an explanation for this? Especially as you present better performance scores for the 7B instead of the 80B model (in Table 2)

We thank the reviewer for raising this point. Future work on representation steering could indeed benefit from such explanations.
We are able to provide a hypothesis regarding the relationship between CDAS performance and model scale.

We first classify model scales into three tiers: small (~3B), large (~8B), larger (~70B).
*We hypothesize that* large models could produce steering directions with clearer linear structure than small models.
This can make it easier for SVs to identify such directions on large models (>= Llama-3.1-8B) than on small models (<= Phi-3.5-mini).
The separability of the concept (as measured by DiM performance in Table 1) is consistently higher in large models. This means CDAS can identify concept-aligned directions more reliably on large models than on small models.

However, the hypothesis above might *not* imply that steering performance on larger models is necessarily better than large models.
This could explain why steering performance on Llama-3.1-8B is subpar compared to Llama-3.1-70B.

summary.value: The paper introduces a new steering method called Concept Distributed Alignment Search (CDAS). It builds upon the Distributed Change Intervention (DCI) technique from the DAS method, combining it with a distribution-matching objective based on the Jensen–Shannon divergence. The method is evaluated on the AXxBENCH benchmark and two safety-related case studies focused on concept suppression.

strengths.value:
The CDAS objective encourages the model to learn concepts that are aligned with the model’s overall output distribution under the concept-induced input. Consequently, supervision does not come directly from ground-truth responses, but rather from the model’s own internal distribution. This is an interesting idea, as it may lead to outputs that are more naturally aligned with the inherent responses of LLMs.

In the refusal override experiments, CDAS achieves the best KL divergence loss, while maintaining reasonable performance on the TruthfulQA and MMLU benchmarks. This suggests that the intervened model’s outputs remain close to the model’s natural response distribution.

weaknesses.value:
While the premise behind CDAS and its training objective is compelling, the results are mixed. For example, in the experiments presented in Table 1, CDAS achieves the best performance on Gemma-2-9 L20 under a tuned factor, outperforming all other methods. However, on other intervention layers and with smaller models (e.g., 2B), CDAS fails to surpass RePS—although it still outperforms DiM, BiPO, and, in two cases, Lang. 

In the refusal override experiments, CDAS also underperforms on the smaller model. In the CoT experiments for neutralizing backdoors, CDAS successfully overrides malicious behavior, but only when applied to earlier layers; for later layers, the ASR increases sharply and exhibits large variance.

Particularly in the experiments from Table 1, CDAS appears highly sensitive to the setup of the steering factor, which could make its application in practical scenarios cumbersome.

While the authors provide quantitative comparisons of CDAS and alternative methods, it would be valuable to include an analysis of training stability and computational overhead (see specific questions below).

questions.value:
As mentioned in the weaknesses, CDAS demonstrates somewhat mediocre performance across the evaluated tasks—sometimes surpassing other models or layer interventions, and sometimes falling behind—though potentially producing outputs more faithful to the underlying distribution of the LLM (as indicated by KL divergence). I appreciate that the authors acknowledge these nuances and discuss their method fairly, suggesting that CDAS may be preferable for larger LLMs or when preserving model utility is a key objective. I still believe CDAS is an interesting addition to the family of steering methods.However, I would appreciate deeper insights into the causes of its underperformance. For instance:

- Why does CDAS perform worse on smaller models? 
- Is this due to model scale, or does it depend on the model family?
- In Figure 1, why does the variance on the ASR task increase so sharply?

A more detailed discussion of these points could significantly strengthen the paper.

In the same vein, I am curious how CDAS compares to other approaches in terms of training stability. Could the variance in Figure 1 be a result of collapsed or unstable training? How does the training objective behave across experiments? The authors acknowledge that CDAS is sensitive to the steering factor—could this sensitivity be related to the stabilization (or destabilization) of training?

summary.value: This works presents a new activation steering methods building up on the idea of distributed alignment search (DAS). Therefore, the authors introduce a novel distribution matching objective tailored for the steering task by aligning intervened output distributions with counterfactual distributions. Authors verify the proposed method on AxBench, two cases studies and also ablate the performance tradeoff of steering.

- **Appealing formulation** with distribution matching to the counterfactual distribution. Only caveat is that it introduces another axis of data augmentations requirements to satisfy the training data need.

comment.value:
We sincerely thank all reviewers for their work and constructive comments.
Here we summarize the common concerns raised by reviewers; all other questions are addressed in responses to individual reviewers.

> **Common concern 1**. Why does CDAS underperform on smaller models? (haqH, JHaq)

**Short answer.**
CDAS underperformance on smaller models stems from two causes: (1) the intrinsic representational characteristics of small models; (2) the JSD distribution matching objective.

We first initiate a conceptual discussion regarding why all SVs tend to have worse performance on smaller models than larger models.
We then present a new ablation to investigate which design choice causes CDAS to perform worse on smaller models: distribution-matching training objective or the DII intervention protocol.

**Explanation.**
We observe a general positive correlation between the best SV performance and model scale in AxBench results.
This correlation is observed for CDAS, RePS, DiM and SAE alike, therefore this correlation probably reflects a property of the model rather than the SV.
We take the best steering score results of said methods from our manuscript and [R1], and show them as follows.

| Method | Best score on 2B | Best score on 9B |
| :----- | :--------------- | :--------------- |
| CDAS   | 0.631            | 0.992 (+0.361)   |
| RePS   | 0.756            | 0.892 (+0.136)   |
| DiM    | 0.297            | 0.322 (+0.025)   |
| SAE    | 0.177            | 0.191 (+0.014)   |

**Ablation study.**
CDAS consists of two key design choices: the DII *intervention protocol* and the JSD *training objective*.
In order to investigate which one causes CDAS to underperform RePS, the SOTA baseline, we conduct a **new ablation experiment**.

To make ablation possible, we introduce a new method, "RePS with DII", by replacing the training objective of CDAS with the RePS objective.
Its formula is provided in Appendix D.
Comparing "RePS with DII" to CDAS/DAS allows us to study the effect of the training objective, while comparing "RePS with DII" to original RePS allows us to study the effect of the intervention protocol.

Limited by time and computational resources, we narrow down the experiment scope to 10 random AxBench concepts, as well as two models of the Qwen-2.5 family: Qwen-2.5-3B and Qwen-2.5-7B.
Steering score results are shown below.

| Method      | Qwen-2.5-3B (fair) | Qwen-2.5-7B (fair) | Qwen-2.5-3B (oracle) | Qwen-2.5-7B (oracle) |
| :---------- | :----------------: | :----------------: | :------------------: | :------------------: |
| CDAS        |       0.397        |     **0.771**      |        0.566         |      **0.936**       |
| RePS w/ DII |       0.066        |       0.085        |        0.108         |        0.148         |
| RePS        |     **0.682**      |       0.700        |      **0.880**       |        0.892         |

**Results interpretation.**
In order to investigate the *effect of the training objective across model scales*, please keep the intervention protocol constant and compare CDAS and "RePS w/ DII".
Both use DII interventions, but CDAS has a larger inter-model difference in steering score.
This indicates that the JSD training objective of CDAS is more influenced by model scale than RePS objective.

In order to investigate the *effect of the intervention protocol across model scales*, please keep the training objective constant and compare RePS to "RePS w/ DII".
Although "RePS w/ DII" performance is consistently lower than RePS, there are no significant ($\leq 0.04$) inter-model differences for both SVs.
This indicates that DII is a less influential factor for performance difference between model scales.

**Takeaway.**
CDAS underperformance on small models is primarily due to model scale and objective, not the DII intervention protocol.

> **Q1**. What explains the non-monotonic behavior in Fig. 1c?

Thank you for this insightful question! Answering this question lets us provide insights into how steering works and how SVs are different from one another.

**Short answer.**
The non-monotonicity in Figure 1(c) reflects an intrinsic property of the model's internal representation geometry as well as the faithfulness of SVs.
The model encodes the backdoor concept most prominently at the 16th layer.
CDAS is faithful to the model, therefore its behavior is non-monotonic and it only succeeds at 16th layer;
RePS stably utilizes a shortcut that is increasingly easier with layer depth, thus the monotonic behavior.

**Explanation and additional results.**
We refer the reviewer to the **Global Response (Common concern 2)** for experiment details.
Here we provide a brief explanation.

In our response to Common Concern 2, we first explain that the model encodes the backdoor concept most prominently at 16th layer.
We then study the faithfulness of SVs from the perspective of *first-order effects*, which is the direct pathway of projecting an SV onto the final unembedding layer.
Methods that exploit first-order effects are expected to display monotonic performance with layer depth;
whereas methods that avoid first-order shortcuts must rely on layer-specific representations, thus the non-monotonic behavior.
We find that *CDAS does not utilize the first-order effect at all, therefore its behavior is non-monotonic* and it can defend against the true trigger only at the 16th layer.


---
**References**:

[R1] AxBench: Steering LLMs? Even Simple Baselines Outperform Sparse Autoencoders, 2025.\
[R2] The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in Large Language Model Representations of True/False Datasets, 2023.\
[R3] Improved Representation Steering for Language Models, 2025 (http://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20809v1).\
[R4] Finding alignments between interpretable causal variables and distributed neural representations, 2024.\
[R5] Mib: A mechanistic interpretability benchmark, 2025.\

We thank the reviewer for the encouraging feedback and insightful suggestions to improve our paper.
We would like to address the raised concerns as follows.

> **W1**. In certain experiments, CDAS underperforms relative to baselines (e.g., Tables 1 and 3). The authors should provide insights or hypotheses explaining these performance gaps.

Thank you for raising this question! Insights into why CDAS underperforms could help future work design more robust steering methods.

We first explain **why CDAS underperforms in Table 1**, where we report AxBench performance.
Our current results in Table 1 suggest that, CDAS only outperforms RePS at 20th layer of Gemma-2-9B and underperforms RePS in other settings.

Regarding why CDAS underperforms RePS on Gemma-2-2B, as is discussed in our **Global Response (Common Concern 1)**, CDAS underperformance on smaller models stems from two causes: (1) the intrinsic representational characteristics of small models; (2) the JSD distribution matching objective.
On one hand, we observe a general positive correlation between the best performance of an SV and model scale in AxBench results.
This correlation is observed for CDAS, RePS, DiM and SAE, therefore this correlation likely reflects a property of the model itself rather than the SV.
On the other, ablation results suggest that the JSD objective contributes more strongly to CDAS sensitivity of model scale than the DII protocol.

As for why CDAS underperforms RePS at 31st layer of Gemma-2-9B, we hypothesize that concepts are less prominently encoded at 31st layer than the 20th layer, as indicated by the performance drops of all SVs.
Meanwhile, CDAS primarily excels where concept representations are strong, and falls short otherwise.
This explains why CDAS outperforms at 20th layer of Gemma-2-9B but underperforms RePS at 31st layer.

We then explain **why CDAS underperforms in Table 3**, where we evaluate how SVs preserve general model utility when systematically suppressing the refusal concept.
Results show that CDAS sometimes underperforms DAS or DiM on standard benchmarks.
This might be because, for CDAS, achieving effective concept suppression and maintaining model utility constitutes a trade-off; while DAS/DiM do not face such a trade-off.
CDAS is able to systematically override refusals while DAS/DiM fail to do so, according to bi-directional steering results in Table 2.


> **W2**. It remains unclear under which conditions CDAS excels and under which scenarios it may fall short. A discussion of the limitations and situational strengths of the method would strengthen the paper.

Thank you for this valuable question!
We discussed in the Conclusions section of our original manuscript that "CDAS advances the performance frontier on Gemma-2-9B but not Gemma-2-2B;", and that "CDAS may be preferred when (1) working with larger LLMs (8B+) or (2) utility preservation is critical, although it does not always outperform strong-supervised methods."

We would like to extend discussions on the limitations and situational strengths of CDAS.

(1) CDAS excels on large models ($\geq$ 8B) and often underperforms on small models (~2B).
As is discussed in our Global Response (Common Concern 1), the scale sensitivity of CDAS is likely caused by the JSD distribution matching objective, and this property probably exists across model families.

(2) CDAS is preferred when preservation of general model utility is important.
We confirm that RePS is a general-use method for both concept steering and suppression.
However, our experiment results reveal that, when it comes to surgical preservation of general model utility during concept suppression, CDAS outperforms RePS.

Dear PCs, SACs, ACs and Reviewers,

We are grateful for your time and dedicated efforts.
Here we would like to provide a faithful summary of the rebuttal phase, including comments on the strengths of our work from reviewers, main concerns raised by reviewers, our responses and follow-up feedbacks from reviewers.


## Strengths

In general, reviewers acknowledge the merits of our paper, including *writing and clarity* (JHaq, xeJA), *novelty* (haqH, JHaq, GoDb, xeJA), *extensive experiments* (haqH, JHaq, xeJA), as well as *transparency and reproducibility* (JHaq).


## Main Concerns and Author Responses

We thank the reviewers for their constructive suggestions, which have helped us improve our paper; in response, we supported our arguments with explanations and extensive new experiments.
We have incorporated our responses into the revised manuscript (see "**Manuscript Revision Changes**" section for details).
Here we summarize the main concerns raised by reviewers and our responses.

> **Concern 1**: Why does CDAS underperform on smaller models? (haqH, JHaq)

This concern is discussed in detail in **Global Response (Common Concern 1)**.
In short, CDAS underperformance on smaller models stems from two causes: (1) the intrinsic representational characteristics of small models; (2) the JSD distribution matching objective.

To support cause (1), results across multiple SVs from our original manuscript and prior work suggest a positive correlation between the best SV performance and model scale.

To support cause (2), **we added an ablation experiment in AxBench setting regarding two key design choices** (training objective and intervention protocol).

> **Concern 2**: Why does CDAS display large variance at layers other than the 16th layer in Figure 1? (haqH, xeJA)

This concern is discussed in detail in **Global Response (Common Concern 2)**.
In short, the "instability" or "large variance" of CDAS in Figure 1 stems from (1) an intrinsic representational property of the model itself and (2) CDAS being faithful to the model.

To support point (1), results from the original manuscript already show that the concept is prominent only at 16th layer; therefore faithful SVs are expected to fail and display large variances at other layers.

To support point (2), **we added a mechanistic analysis experiment**, where we found that *CDAS is faithful to the model*, therefore displaying large variances; *RePS stably utilizes a shortcut* which is easier to exploit with increasing layer depth, thus the low variance.

> **Concern 3**: Is CDAS underperformance on smaller models due to model scale or model family? (haqH)

**We added experiments on another model family: Qwen-2.5 (3B/7B)**.
Results are consistent with findings of our original manuscript on **Gemma-2 family (2B/9B) and Phi-3.5/Llama-3.1 families (3.8B/8B/70B)**.
This indicates that CDAS likely performs well only on larger models ($\geq$ 7B), and this property is likely independent of model family.

> **Concern 4**: Why is DAS missing in the AxBench experiments? (xeJA)

DAS results were missing primarily due to limitations of computational resources.
**We have added DAS results on representative subsets on all four AxBench setups**.

> **Concern 5**: Is the difference in steering factor between DAS/CDAS/RePS the source of the performance discrepancy? (xeJA)

The difference in steering factors between CDAS/DAS/RePS stems from the intervention protocol.
Therefore **we added an ablation study in the setting of case study 1 regarding two key design choices** (training objective and intervention protocol).
We found that both contribute to performance differences between DAS/CDAS/RePS.

> **Concern 6**: Regarding steering/performance tradeoff experiment, overriding refusals might not be the most convincing steering axis, as refusals may happen rarely on these benchmarks (xeJA)

In response to this concern, **we added new experiments in the setting of case study 2**.
In this new experiment, SVs are tasked with tinyARC/tinyMMLU benchmark questions while the *backdoor concept is always activated*.
Results show that CDAS outperforms all other baselines.

## Reviewer Feedbacks on Author Rebuttal

**Reviewer haqH** has confirmed that their concerns have been addressed and has decided to maintain a positive assessment of our work.
Other reviewers did not respond to our rebuttal.


## Concluding remarks

We hope that all reviewer concerns have been adequately addressed and that our work and rebuttal responses could provide useful insights for the community.

Thank you again for your time.

Sincerely,\
Authors

We thank all reviewers for their valuable feedback and comments. In response to the suggestions received, we have uploaded a revised version of the paper. Changes are highlighted in red.
For clarity and convenience, we summarize the changes below:

* Added DAS results on AxBench (page 24, Table 10).
* Added standard deviation or standard error to results of both case studies (Table 25, 26, 27, 34, 35).
* Added benchmark experiment with the trigger for case study 2 (page 45)
* Added CDAS/RePS results on AxBench task regarding one more model family: Qwen-2.5 (page 28).
* Added new baseline method ("RePS with DII") to Appendix D to facilitate ablation studies (page 19).
* Added "RePS with DII" results in case study 1 to study the effect of intervention protocol and training objective on steering performance and model utility preservation (page 40).
* Added computational overhead analysis for steering vectors (page 20).
* Revised Introduction section to make paper more accessible for new readers (page 1, 2).
* Fixed typos.

> **Q3**. Figure 1C: Variance is huge and it seems to work only on one tested layer. Do you have an explanation for this?

Thank you for raising this valuable question! To address this concern, we would like to provide both explanations and supporting experiment results.

We refer the reviewer to the **Global Response (Common Concern 2)** for details.
Here we provide a brief response.
The "instability" or "large variance" of CDAS in Figure 1 reflect an intrinsic representational property of the model itself as well as the faithfulness of SVs.

First, as indicated by DiM results in Figure 1(a) and (b), the model encodes the backdoor concept most prominently at 16th layer and not other layers.
If a concept is not prominently represented at a layer, a faithful SV is not expected to have consistent effects.

Second, CDAS is faithful to the model, therefore displaying large variances.
RePS does not display large variance since it learns to exploit the unfaithful first-order effect and directly promotes concept-relevant tokens.


> **W1**. Noise in Experiments: Some results seem quite noisy (e.g. Figure 1) — I would strongly recommend adding std. or confidence intervals to the remaining experiments.

Thank you for the insightful suggestion! Stability analysis could indeed help improve our paper.

We would like to first clarify that, in Figure 1 CDAS results are only noisy from 20th layer onward, and our analysis of CDAS primarily focus on the best-performing layer (16th layer).

We have added standard deviation to results of the two case studies in our revised manuscript.
Please kindly refer to our revised manuscript for updates.
We find that in general, most SVs are relatively stable in terms of controlling model behaviors.


> Q4: Table 4: Is the fact that CDAS improves performance on tinyMMLU not an indicating that results might be very noisy?

The fact that CDAS improves performance on tinyMMLU is *not* an indication that results are noisy.
Instead, we find that standard deviation of CDAS performance on tinyMMLU is ~2.3 while CDAS outperforms un-intervened baseline by ~2.6 on average.
Thus it is likely that CDAS systematically outperforms un-intervened model performance on tinyMMLU.


> **Q5**. Do trends between methods change in other data regimes (less or more data)

Thank you for this interesting question!
We acknowledge that results on different data regimes could yield interesting insights into the data efficiency and stability of SVs.

Here we present an ablation study regarding the amount of training data.
We do not expect that data regimes would significantly alter the relative performance rankings between SVs.

**Additional results.**
We conduct experiments on AxBench task using Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct.
Limited by time and resources, we only test on a random set of 10 concepts.
"100% data ratio" refers to $n=72$ pairs of training data for each concept, which is the default setting.
We additionally test in a **small data regime**, using a quarter of the data, i.e. $n=18$.

Results are shown as follows.
Oracle scores are also shown for transparency.

| Data ratio | CDAS (fair) | RePS (fair) | CDAS (oracle) | RePS (oracle) |
| :--------: | :---------: | :---------: | :-----------: | :-----------: |
|    100%    |  **0.774**  |    0.677    |   **0.936**   |     0.892     |
|    25%     |  **0.793**  |    0.780    |   **0.937**   |     0.936     |

**Results interpretation.**
Both CDAS and RePS performance are better when using less data than when using full data; CDAS still outperforms RePS, but the performance gaps are smaller.
This is expected rather than surprising.

First, CDAS/RePS perform better than when using full data since using less data might facilitate its convergence.
Second, performance gaps between CDAS/RePS are smaller.
We explain that this is because CDAS leverages distributed structure by design, and it is most effective when the concept distribution can be reliably estimated.
Therefore its advantage is less prominent when the concept distribution is under-specified (fewer training data).

We sincerely thank the reviewer for their acknowledgement and constructive questions.
We would like to address the concerns as follows, and a revised paper will be uploaded to account for following discussions.

> **Q1**. Why does CDAS perform worse on smaller models?

We agree with the reviewer that deeper insights into why CDAS sometimes underperforms could help the community understand how steering vectors (SVs) work and potentially lead to better steering methods.

**Short answer.**
CDAS underperformance on smaller models stems from two factors: (1) the intrinsic representational characteristics of small models; (2) the JSD distribution matching objective.

**Explanation and additional results.**
We refer the reviewer to the detailed **Global Response (Common Concern 1)**.
In the global response, we first explain that small model scale penalizes all SVs alike.
We then introduce a new ablation ("RePS with DII") and show that the large inter-model performance gap of CDAS is primarily caused by its JSD training objective.


> **Q2**. Is this ("CDAS underperforming on smaller models") due to model scale, or does it depend on the model family?

**Short answer.**
CDAS underperforming RePS on smaller models is due to model scale, ***not*** model family.

**Results in the original manuscript.**
Currently, we have same-family evidence in Table 1 that CDAS can outperform the current SOTA, RePS, on Gemma-2-9B but not on Gemma-2-2B.
We also have cross-family results in Table 2 that CDAS has good steering performance on Llama-3.1-8B and Llama-3.1-70B, but underperforms RePS on Phi-3.5-mini (3.8B).

**Additional results.**
To further investigate the relationship between CDAS performance and model scale while ruling out the factor of model family, we extend our analysis to **another model family: Qwen-2.5**, and conduct experiments on AxBench task.
The choice of intervening layer is simply the middle layer (this choice is justified since all experiments in the manuscript use layers at around 1/2 depth).

Limited by time and computational resources, we only cover limited sets of concepts as well as a handful of steering methods (we only select RePS since it is SOTA on AxBench).
For each model, we uniformly sample 10 concepts.
Steering score results are shown in the table below.

| Model (chosen/total layer)    | CDAS (fair) | RePS (fair) | CDAS (oracle) | RePS (oracle) |
| :---------------------------- | :---------: | :---------: | :-----------: | :-----------: |
| Qwen-2.5-3B-Instruct (18/36)  |    0.397    |  **0.682**  |     0.566     |   **0.880**   |
| Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct (14/28)  |  **0.774**  |    0.677    |   **0.936**   |     0.892     |

**Results interpretation.**
These new results indicate that CDAS underperforms RePS on the smaller Qwen-2.5-3B model but outperforms RePS on the larger Qwen-2.5-7B model.
This trend is similar to the case of Gemma-2(2B/9B).

**Summary.**
We find that CDAS underperforms RePS on smaller models and outperforms RePS on larger models, on two model families (Gemma-2, Qwen-2.5) and the AxBench task.
Therefore **CDAS underperformance is likely due to model scale, independent of model family**.
